derivationStages.stageRecord: Project IP with every student base-generated in Spec-IP and VP as the complement of I. This adopts the traditional GB external-subject configuration rather than a VP-internal subject derivation. The predicate assigns its external Agent role to the subject. Finite I licenses nominative Case on that NP through the Spec-head relation. I carries past tense and third-person singular agreement, licensing the selected past form read without head movement or affix lowering. I is unpronounced. The resulting pronounced terminals reproduce the input; an additional CP shell is not required for this independent declarative.

derivationStages.stageRecord: Apply clause-bounded Quantifier Raising to a book, adjoining an upper occurrence to IP. The earlier workspace supplies the object position from which this dependency is formed. This GB LF analysis uses copy notation: the upper NP is unpronounced and interpreted as the existential operator, while the pronounced lower NP is interpreted as its bound variable. Thus covert movement does not alter the input's word order. The operator c-commands its lower occurrence; the lower occurrence remains the theta- and Case-bearing position of the chain. Raising the object first supplies an intermediate IP to which the universal subject can subsequently adjoin.

Its pronounced lower occurrence is interpreted as a bound variable and retains the subject chain's theta-role and Case licensing. This second clause-bounded A-bar dependency crosses no island. The upper universal now asymmetrically c-commands the upper existential, establishing universal-over-existential scope. The completed reading says that each student read at least one book, with the book potentially varying between students; it does not require different books. Only the lower occurrences are pronounced, so the completed workspace still spells Every student read a book.

cases.sentence: Pat is a Republican and proud of it.

values.interpretation: content or object of pride

derivationStages.stageRecord: In a classical NP-based X-bar analysis, Pat projects an NP, while a occupies the determiner position of the predicate nominal a Republican. Republican is therefore a noun here, not the adjective found in an expression such as very Republican. Proud projects an AP and selects the PP of it as its content complement. Within that PP, of selects the pronominal NP and assigns it objective Case under government. These local dependencies are established before the predicates acquire their shared subject. The coordinated predicates will differ in category, but both can function as predicates of an individual.
derivationStages.statement: Construct the subject and the two predicative expressions.

values.interpretation: conjunction of Republican membership and pride

values.externalArgument: one shared subject of the coordinated predicate
values.nominalStatus: predicative, not an independently Case-marked object

values.discourseInterpretation: normally Pat's being a Republican; a contextual antecedent is also possible without structural change
values.requirement: the pronoun is not locally bound by Pat

derivationStages.stageRecord: And heads a binary ConjP, with the nominal predicate as its specifier and the adjectival predicate as its complement. The coordination is licensed by their shared predicative function rather than identical category labels: it attributes Republican membership and pride to one individual. A silent Pred head embeds this coordination, and Pat is merged in its specifier. PredP is the explicit X-bar implementation of the small clause; the coordinated predicate supplies one shared external argument position, rather than assigning Pat two independent argument positions. The copula is then merged in V and selects this PredP without assigning a further external theta-role. Finite present I projects above VP, leaving its subject position unfilled at this stage. The predicate nominal is not an independent object receiving accusative Case. It is part of the predication over Pat. The pronoun it must be locally free under Binding Principle B: Pat cannot locally bind it in this predication. Its natural interpretation is discourse-anaphoric to Pat's being a Republican, not syntactic binding by the predicate nominal; a contextually supplied referent would not change the structure.
derivationStages.statement: Coordinate the predicates and establish the underlying copular clause.

values.representation: pronounced raised head and silent head trace

values.coordinationConstraint: no extraction from an individual conjunct

relations.relation: Binding Principle B after subject movement

values.interpretation: discourse anaphora does not establish a syntactic binding chain
values.requirement: it remains free of local binding by the Pat chain

derivationStages.stageRecord: The copula moves from its previously established V position to finite I, leaving a silent head trace. This is the ordinary V-to-I behavior of English finite be; it crosses no intervening head. The lexical terminal is retains its supplied inflected form, so this analysis requires no separate spelling operation. Pat then undergoes A-movement from the small-clause subject position to Spec-IP, leaving an NP trace. The landing position satisfies the finite clause's subject requirement, and finite I licenses nominative Case on the subject chain and singular agreement with Pat. The chain receives its thematic interpretation only at its small-clause origin, so the non-thematic copula and the higher subject position introduce no additional theta-role. The subject's relation to both conjuncts was established outside the coordination; neither movement extracts an element from just one conjunct. Principle B continues to require that it not be locally bound by the subject chain. The resulting IP is a complete declarative analysis of the exact input. It coordinates predicates, not two independently asserted clauses, and does not posit an unpronounced repetition of Pat is.
derivationStages.statement: Raise the copula and subject to complete the finite sentence.

cases.sentence: John left, and Mary did too.

values.interpretation: conjunction
Mary, in addition to John, left

derivationStages.stageRecord: The analysis uses IP for the finite clause and a headed coordination projection whose specifier is the first IP and whose complement is the second IP. Subjects are base-generated in Spec-IP, as in a classical GB implementation without VP-internal subject raising. Each occurrence of leave assigns its external Agent theta-role to its clause's subject through predication. Each finite I assigns nominative Case to that subject, and both I heads bear past tense. And coordinates the two finite propositions. Too is right-adjoined to the second IP, outside the VP that will undergo ellipsis. Its additive interpretation associates with Mary: the proposition that Mary left is added to the already available proposition that John left. The two verbs remain uninflected at this syntactic stage; their surface realizations have not yet been established.
derivationStages.statement: Construct coordinated finite clauses with clause-adjoined additive too.

values.operation: suppress pronunciation of the second VP while retaining its syntax

derivationStages.stageRecord: The second clause's VP is identified with the first clause's VP: both contain the same intransitive predicate leave. VP ellipsis suppresses pronunciation of the second VP without removing its syntactic or theta-interpretive content. Consequently, Mary retains its theta-role, and the second finite I remains outside the deletion domain. Too also remains pronounced because its clause-adjoined position is outside that domain. This PF deletion precedes the choice of tense realization: the second lexical verb is no longer available as a pronounced host for past tense, whereas the first verb remains available. No subject or verb has moved in this stage.
derivationStages.statement: Suppress pronunciation of the second VP under antecedent identity.

relations.relation: PF tense lowering and head adjunction

values.chain: past-tense head and its silent source trace
values.operation: lower past tense from I to V at PF
insert supportive do in I after VP ellipsis

A silent trace remains in I; the original tense occurrence is retained at the landing site, and both positions belong to the same chain. The resulting verbal complex is realized suppletively as left. In the second clause, the already established VP ellipsis prevents tense from being realized on a pronounced lexical verb. Supportive do is therefore inserted under I and combines with the retained past-tense head; that complex is realized as did. This is support insertion, not movement of do from the deleted VP. The resulting finite auxiliary licenses the overt auxiliary–silent VP configuration. The full silent VP remains available for interpretation and preserves Mary's theta-role. Too remains outside the ellipsis domain, and its clause-level additive association is unchanged. The realization groups record the two irregular inflected forms; the remaining pronounced terminals supply John, and, Mary, and too in their written order.

values.implementation: The inflected lexical verb remains in V.

derivationStages.stageRecord: The embedded clause is projected as IP, using the traditional GB analysis in which its subject is generated in Spec-IP. The wh-phrase who initially occupies that argument position. Broke projects a V-bar with the definite NP the window as its complement; the determiner occupies the nominal specifier position. Broke assigns its agent role to who and its patient role to the window. Finite I licenses nominative Case on the subject, while the verb governs and assigns accusative Case to its object. Broke is lexically inserted in its past-tense form and is licensed by abstract past I; no embedded verb movement or subsequent spelling operation is assumed.

derivationStages.stageRecord: A CP shell is projected over the existing IP, and who moves from the previously represented subject position to Spec-CP. The landing occurrence retains the NP's identity; a silent NP trace marks its former position. The null C licenses this relative-type operator dependency. The movement is local within the embedded clause and does not cross an intervening subject or an island. The agent relation is now anchored at the subject trace rather than at the operator's landing position. Nominative Case is likewise assigned at that subject position and licensed on the pronounced operator through its chain; the object's accusative licensing remains unchanged. The resulting CP denotes an open proposition whose missing agent is represented by the subject trace.

derivationStages.stageRecord: The matrix IP is assembled with nonreferential it in Spec-IP, abstract past I, and a copular VP. John is the copula's nominal focus complement. The already constructed CP is attached to the outer V-bar, outside the lower V-bar containing the copula and John; it is not a restrictive modifier inside John's NP. This is a base-generated, construction-specific cleft analysis: John has not moved out of the embedded clause. The cleft dependency identifies John as the value of the open agent variable in the CP and treats the CP as the cleft's background proposition. Matrix I assigns nominative Case to it. The copula licenses John as a predicative focus nominal, not as an accusative object; expletive it receives no independent thematic role. Was is inserted as the past form of be, with head movement still pending.

Its pronounced occurrence retains its identity, while a silent V trace occupies its former position. The resulting complex I contains was and the unpronounced tense head; no morphological fusion or respelling is needed because was was already the selected past-tense lexical form. Nonreferential it does not bind John, and the semantic focus dependency is not an A-binding relation from it to the name. The completed tree therefore yields the cleft reading: it is John, rather than a contextually relevant alternative, who broke the window. The pronounced terminals now spell the exact input in order.
